steps.body: To order a whole set of decimals, use one trick: **pad them all to the same number of places** with trailing zeros, then read them like whole numbers. Once every number has the same length, the smallest "whole number" is the least decimal.
Ordering decimals is reading positions, not counting digits.

widget.prompt: Place 0.45. Then ask yourself whether it is bigger or smaller than 0.5.
widget.successFeedback: 0.45 sits just BELOW 0.5, even though it has more digits. More digits does not mean bigger — 0.45 is 45 hundredths and 0.5 is 50 hundredths, and the line settles the argument instantly.

predict.prompt: Before you place it: is 0.45 closer to 0 or to 1?
predict.reveal: 0.45 sits 0.45 from 0 and 0.55 from 1 — the 0 side wins. Judging position from the endpoints first makes the exact placement easier to defend.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents order decimals.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for order decimals must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines order decimals.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

commonErrors.feedback: Pad to 0.50: it's bigger than 0.45. The least is 0.45.
0.54 is the largest of the three, not the least. The least is 0.45.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Pad all three to hundredths — 0.45, 0.50, 0.54 — then compare 45, 50, 54.
widget.successFeedback: Padded to 0.45, 0.50, 0.54 — 45 is smallest, so 0.45 is least.

steps.body: The padding trick shines when lengths are mixed. For 0.3, 0.25, 0.301, 0.31, pad to three places: 0.300, 0.250, 0.301, 0.310. Now compare 300, 250, 301, 310 — the order falls right out.

explanationVariants: As thousandths 250, 300, 301, 310: the second smallest is 300 = 0.3.

widget.prompt: In 0.3, 0.25, 0.301, 0.31 ordered least to greatest, which comes SECOND?

commonErrors.feedback: 0.25 is the smallest — it comes first, not second. Second is 0.3.
0.31 (310) is the largest — it comes last. Second is 0.3.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Pad to thousandths — 300, 250, 301, 310 — then order them and take the second smallest.
widget.successFeedback: Padded to thousandths: 250, 300, 301, 310. Second smallest is 300 = 0.3.

misorderFeedback.feedback: Pad to 0.409 vs 0.400: 409 is bigger than 400, so 0.4 comes before 0.409.
Pad to 0.400 vs 0.380: 400 is bigger than 380, so 0.38 comes before 0.4.

hints: Pad the whole set to the same length first.
explanationVariants: As hundredths 9, 90, 19 — 90 wins, so 0.9 is greatest.

commonErrors.feedback: 0.19 looks long, but pad 0.9 to 0.90: 90 beats 19. The greatest is 0.9.
0.09 is the smallest of the three. Padded, 0.90 is greatest: 0.9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Pad to hundredths — 90, 19, 9 — the biggest padded number is the greatest decimal.
widget.successFeedback: Padded to 0.90, it's 90 hundredths — bigger than 0.19 (19) and 0.09 (9). 0.9 is greatest.

steps.body: Same length, then read as whole numbers.
takeaways: Pad every decimal to the same number of places with trailing zeros.
Then compare and order them exactly like whole numbers.
This handles mixed-length sets (0.3 vs 0.301) without any guesswork.
steps.teaser: next chapter: rounding decimals to a chosen place.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Give every decimal the same number of places (pad with trailing zeros), then compare like whole numbers.** For 0.5 and 0.42, pad to 0.50 and 0.42 → compare 50 and 42 → 0.42 is smaller. Equal lengths make ordering easy.

explanationVariants: Padded to 0.50 and 0.42, 42 < 50, so 0.42 is least.

options.feedback: Pad to 0.50 vs 0.42: 42 < 50, so 0.42 is less.
Pad 0.5 to 0.50: 50 is bigger than 42, so 0.5 is the greater one. 0.42 is less.

options.label: Equal
options.feedback: Padded to 0.50 and 0.42 they differ (50 vs 42), so 0.42 is less.
